Why do uncertainties matter, first of all?
Well, uncertainties matter because no physical measurement in real life is exact.
Every single measurement is limited by something.
For example, instrument precision, or experimental technique, or environmental errors.
So, environment.
And because physics relies on a lot of measured data, each value has to include an uncertainty.
And without it, you can't really do it effectively.
A measurement is written as x equals x measured plus minus the uncertainty.
For example, let's say you want to measure the length of a book.
You could say the length would be equal to 12.4 plus minus 0.1 centimetres.
And this is the uncertainty.
This basically tells the readers, or the examiner, that your book has a length between 12.3 and 12.5.

There's random uncertainty and systematic uncertainty.
Both of these are really stressed in IB.
If you're doing AP, this is probably not going to be that important.
But if you're doing IB and you're going to be doing labs, this is very, very important to know.
Random uncertainty is caused by unpredictable fluctuations.
And it varies from trial to trial.
For example, when you're doing a stopwatch, there could be a difference in reaction time.
However, systematic uncertainty is a consistent error, or a consistent bias, in one direction.
And it can't be reduced by repetition, while random can be reduced by repetition.

while a random uncertainty is basically the more you do the experiment, the less random uncertainty there will be.

Velocity is distance over time.

you want to first take the percentage uncertainty.

The percent uncertainty for distance would be one, let's say, or 0.1 metres would be a more reasonable uncertainty.

The total uncertainty would be 0.4, 0.42.

Once you have all the uncertainties required for division or multiplication, you could just add the uncertainties.

So once you calculate what your final velocity is, you would get 2.1 metres per second.
You would take this 2.4 uncertainty and you would put it into here.
So if you do this, divided by 100 times 2.1, you get an uncertainty of plus minus 0.04 metres per second.
And that would be your final answer.
Make sure that your final digit also matches the uncertainty here.
So you would have to add an extra figure here.
But basically that's how you calculate uncertainties when you're dividing and multiplying.
What if you're adding two values?
Let's say you want to add two distances, 5.0 plus minus 0.1 metres, 0.1 metres.
And then you add that with another distance calculation, let's say 6.0 plus minus 0.2 metres.
Well, when you're adding or subtracting, it's way easier than when you have to multiply and you have to get all the percent uncertainties and adding them.
You could just add the uncertainties directly.
Because if you think about it, these uncertainties cover the ranges of what you have to measure.
So by adding them, you are accounting for both the ranges.
And that's how you calculate uncertainty.
Remember, for multiplying and dividing, you have to convert it to percent uncertainties, add it, and then apply it to your final answer.
However, for adding, you could just directly add the uncertainties.
